title: Deepening (Learning) Understanding - 3
author: Martin Skelton
summary: In this instalment of his learning series, Skelton asks what understanding looks like and concludes that it is rarely visible. Unlike knowledge and skills, it is not learned through telling or coaching but through reflection that needs space and time, and it matures as the pre-frontal cortex develops. He contrasts a 17-year-old in Guadalajara whose wall slogan turned out to rest on genuine, long-simmered reflection with a bright eleven-year-old whose profound remark was simply her mother's words repeated. The lesson is to ask what has brought a student to say something, because clever remarks and high-level skills can both masquerade as understanding. Drawing on Wiggins and McTighe, he adds that understanding is only one aim of schooling and is often inappropriate for young children or for subjects such as second languages.
points: Understanding is learned through reflection given space and time rather than direct telling, so it is seldom observed in a single lesson.
Apparently profound student remarks are often repeated knowledge, and the question what has brought you to say that separates the two.
Mastery of a high-level skill deserves celebration in its own right and should not be relabelled as understanding.
Educators should ask where understanding is a legitimate goal, avoiding the word with young children and in subjects that are chiefly knowledge and skill.
quotes: What I am sure about is that understanding is not learned directly through telling and/or coaching, as are knowledge and skills. I’m also increasingly sure that it is learned differently. It happens when we know how to reflect (a skill that might well be learned from a good coach, from whom we have some good repeated experiences) and are given space and time to do so.
The truth is, you don’t often see it. I have only seen it happen in front of me very occasionally and always over significant periods of time. It’s like spotting the rare bird in the learning forest.
It’s not mine to ‘correct her’. I recognised in what she said the kind of personal truths that I was struggling to make coherent when I was her age. Her reflections were, rightly, hers.
It was something she had been told by her mother and was repeating very effectively. It was knowledge. She had learned something to say when a particular question was asked.

Spending time in hundreds of classrooms with children and students of different ages, I have come to realise that the apparently profound remarks of students of all ages, including older students, are often a repetition of some content told them by their teachers and not the result of their own reflection. The 17 year-old student in Guadalajara might have sat in endless assemblies or lessons where this was said to students with monotonous regularity.
To be able to perform a high level skill at Mastering level should be celebrated for what it is; high level skills learning. It isn’t necessarily understanding.

If I were back running a primary/elementary school I would do everything I could to suppress the use of the word ‘understand’ with the children. It’s unhelpful, misleading to children, parents and teachers and reduces skills and knowledge to some second division category.
